title: Traditional Marseille soap
subtitle: The classic French 72% olive-oil bar
excerpt: A cold-process Marseille-style soap based on the traditional formula of 72% olive oil, 18% coconut oil, and 10% castor oil, with no added fragrance. Firm, hard-lathering, and long-lasting. Makes 7 bars.
sourceNotes: Marseille soap traditional 72% olive formula: documented in Anne Bramson, Soap: Making It, Enjoying It (1972) and Susan Miller Cavitch, The Soapmaker's Companion (1997), ch. 12. SAP values: SoapCalc table (olive 0.134, coconut 0.190, castor 0.128). 5% superfat, 33% water-to-oil. Note: true Savon de Marseille under French regulation requires industrial production and specific provenance; this is a home version in the traditional formula.

recipe.batchNotes: Run any scale change through a lye calculator before batching.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Allow 4 to 6 weeks minimum cure. Six weeks gives the classic firm, white Marseille bar.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: Three years or more in a cool dark cupboard once fully cured. The high olive-oil content makes the bar resistant to rancidity. Discard if orange spots (DOS) or a sharp paint-like smell appear.

glossaryTerms.definition: The chemical reaction between fat and sodium hydroxide that produces soap and glycerine. Each oil has a SAP value: the grams of lye needed to fully saponify one gram of that oil.
The point at which soap batter has thickened enough that a drizzle on the surface briefly holds its shape. The signal that oils and lye have emulsified and the batter is ready to pour.
The percentage of lye reduced below the full saponification amount to leave a small reserve of unsaponified oil in the finished bar (also called the superfat). This makes the bar gentler on skin.

projectSchedule.title: Unmould and cut
projectSchedule.body: Turn out the loaf. This formula cuts more easily than 100% olive Castile because the coconut oil gives extra hardness. Wear protective gloves: the bar is still caustic.

projectSchedule.title: Turn the bars
projectSchedule.body: Flip each bar on the rack so both sides cure evenly. The bars should be firm enough to handle at this point.

projectSchedule.title: Four-week test
projectSchedule.body: Press a sliver to the tongue. No sting means the soap is fully alkaline-neutralised and safe. The bar is usable from this point.

projectSchedule.title: Six-week cure complete
projectSchedule.body: A fully cured Marseille-style bar is firm, white to pale ivory, and produces a dense, stable lather. Store on an open rack.

content.text: Marseille soap is the traditional French bar of 72% olive oil, with coconut oil for cleansing and lather, and castor oil to stabilise the foam. The formula has no fragrance and no colour. The
lye discount
here is 5%, leaving a small reserve of free oil in the bar. The
saponification
of this oil blend produces a bar that is firm enough to use as a laundry soap and mild enough for daily face and body use. Cure time is four to six weeks.
Put on protective gloves and goggles before handling lye.
Ingredients

items.prepNote: 18% of oil weight; melt gently if solid
10% of oil weight; stabilises and boosts lather

content.text: Method
Mix the lye solution

In a ventilated space, wearing protective gloves and goggles, pour the distilled water into the HDPE lye pitcher. Add the sodium hydroxide to the water in a steady stream, stirring. Never add water to lye. The solution heats sharply; let it cool to 38 to 42°C before proceeding.
Prepare the oils
Melt the coconut oil gently. Combine with the olive oil and castor oil. Cool to 38 to 42°C.
Blend to trace
When both are within a few degrees of each other, pour the lye solution into the oils in a slow stream. Blend with the stick blender in short bursts until the batter reaches light
trace
: thin custard consistency. The high olive content means this may take 10 to 20 minutes of stick blending.
Pour, insulate, unmould, and cure
Pour into the silicone loaf mould. Wrap in a towel. Leave 48 hours. Unmould wearing protective gloves. Cut into bars and cure on a rack in a cool, dry room for 4 to 6 weeks, turning every two weeks.
Storage and shelf life
Three years in a cool dark cupboard on an open rack. The high oleic-acid content of the olive oil makes this bar very resistant to rancidity. Discard if DOS (orange spots) or a sharp smell appear.
